studyMetadata.title: STOP&SCAN Expert Panel
studyMetadata.description: Review how STOP&SCAN is used in four documented cases and compare it with SIFT and with detection and provenance tools.

uiConfig.studyEndMsg: Thank you for completing the STOP&SCAN expert panel. You may close this window.

consent.instruction: Please read the consent document, then confirm in the sidebar.

response.prompt: I have read this document and had the chance to ask questions. I am 18 or older. (Participants in the EEA, UK, or Switzerland) I explicitly consent to my data being processed as described and transferred to the United States.
I consent to take part in this study.

ratings-stopscan.instruction: Rate STOP&SCAN on the statements below. Comments are in the sidebar.

response.prompt: How far do you agree with each statement about STOP&SCAN?
response.secondaryText: About STOP&SCAN as a method, not the person in any case.
questionOptions: R1. The framework includes the right elements and leaves out nothing essential.
R2. It is useful to distinguish the number of steps completed from the number of independent kinds of evidence found.
R3. Requiring two independent kinds of evidence before a resolved conclusion is an appropriate threshold.
R4. A non-expert could tell whether two kinds of evidence are genuinely independent.
R5. “Unresolved” is a realistic result that people would be willing to accept.
R6. STOP&SCAN works as well when real content is called fake as when the content itself is fake.
R7. Separating the evidence state from the action that follows is a useful distinction for non-experts.
R8. A non-expert could tell which kind of situation they are in — information, a request, or an alert.

response.prompt: Comments on any of these statements. Name which one if you can.
response.secondaryText: Name the statement if you can.

response.prompt: Interaction log

ratings-sift.instruction: Rate SIFT on the statements below. We have not yet told you what we think. Comments are in the sidebar.

response.prompt: How far do you agree with each statement about SIFT?
response.secondaryText: About SIFT as a method. We have not yet given our own view.
questionOptions: R9. SIFT remains useful for evaluating content that may be AI-generated or manipulated.
R10. Allowing someone to stop after one SIFT move is appropriate.
R11. SIFT gives enough guidance when a trustworthy source publishes incorrect or fabricated content.
R12. SIFT gives enough guidance when authentic content is wrongly described as AI-generated.
R13. Caulfield’s 2025 SIFT update — using language models as research tools, then checking their sources — is enough for content that may itself have been generated by AI.

response.prompt: Comments on any of these statements. Name which one if you can.
response.secondaryText: Name the statement if you can.

response.prompt: Interaction log

ratings-open.instruction: Open critique, before we state our own positions on SIFT.

response.prompt: Where is STOP&SCAN most likely to fail in everyday use?
response.secondaryText: Including outside these four cases.

response.prompt: Which element is weakest? How would you change it?
response.secondaryText: The element you would change first, and how.

response.prompt: STOP&SCAN asks people to visit every element, even when an earlier one seems to settle the case. Is that right?
response.secondaryText: The framework currently requires visiting every element.

response.prompt: What, if anything, does STOP&SCAN add that SIFT or lateral reading does not already provide?
response.secondaryText: What is new, if anything, compared with SIFT or lateral reading.

response.prompt: What evidence would you need before recommending STOP&SCAN to non-experts?
response.secondaryText: What would make a recommendation responsible.

response.prompt: Is there an approach from your own work that neither framework captures?
response.secondaryText: A practice from your field that neither method covers.

response.prompt: Did our worked examples represent STOP&SCAN fairly, or did they make it look better or worse than it is?
response.secondaryText: Whether our four cases were a fair test.

response.prompt: Interaction log
